title: You could have invented transformers from memory
author: Alex Wang (independent; Stanford PhD, formerly Cartesia)
takeaway: An explainer (about 19 minutes, derivations, a NumPy script and an in-page slider) that reads a linear layer, an MLP and softmax attention as stores of key-value memories and ranks them by how much the other memories leak into a recall. For random unit keys and values at key dimension 64, queried with a stored key, the leak equals the recalled value at about 64 memories for an outer-product matrix, 128 for a least-squares matrix or ReLU MLP, about 2,700 for a squared ReLU and about 1.2 million for softmax at the usual sharpness; our independent run and the author's 5-seed data agree with each.
verdict: Believe the derivations and every number: we recomputed them from scratch and they agree with the author's released data. Read "capacity" as how many rows one readout can hold before crosstalk equals the signal, for random vectors queried exactly, not as how much a layer stores per parameter: the matrix holds its 64 memories in 4,096 numbers, while the MLP's 2,700 and attention's 1.2 million each take their own 128-number row.

headline.k: capacity at key dimension 64: an outer-product matrix holds about d = 64 random memories before interference equals the signal; a squared-ReLU MLP about 2d²/3 = 2,731
headline.d: derived in the article; ours: 67 and 2,853 measured (3 seeds)

headline.k: softmax attention at the usual sharpness β = √64 = 8: capacity e^{2β(1 − β/d)} = e^14; the author's run crosses 1 at about 1.23 million
headline.d: derived, then simulated to 2 million keys

headline.k: interference over signal with 2 million stored memories when the sharpness grows with log M (Su's and Qwen's rules, reference 1,024); without it the ratio passes 1 near 1.2 million
headline.d: the author's simulation, 5 seeds; released data

code.n: crosstalk.py (about 150 lines of NumPy; uv run, under a minute) and data/crosstalk.json, the five-seed curves behind every chart in the post (commit 5defb8d, 15 October 2026; no licence file).

companion.n: The same argument as a talk, titled "Associative memory as a fuzzy perspective on architecture design".

more_note: The interactive bar figure (one recall's weights, with a slider for the number of memories and the sharpness) is in the post under "Recall picks up interference".

responses.t: The memory analogy is weak once training is in the picture
responses.by: a Hacker News commenter, with the author's reply
responses.n: Layers act on deep representations shaped by a loss, so treating Q, K and V as a lookup table says little about what trained layers do; attention is better seen as a kernel method. The author agreed the post is an intuition that ignores what gets written into the weights and the learning dynamics, and pointed to the papers in his closing list.

responses.t: Random keys are white noise; real data has structure
responses.n: The capacities hold for random keys and values; real keys are correlated and real values are structured, which both helps (compression) and hurts (correlated keys interfere more). A second commenter adds that truly random key-value pairs would be served better by an exact associative array. The post states the first limit itself in its closing section.

responses.t: Why not take the hard maximum?
responses.by: a Hacker News commenter, answered in the thread
responses.n: If higher powers suppress interference better, the limit is argmax over keys. The answer, already in the post: argmax is not differentiable, and a very large β saturates the softmax so the gradients to other keys vanish; hence β grows only as fast as M requires.

The largest sub-thread: readers without linear algebra found d_k, ℝ^{d_k}, M and "similarity" not defined at first use and asked for a worked example with real data structures; others answered that the terms paragraph defines them. A reading-level complaint, not an error.

resources.t: Attention Is All You Need, arXiv v2 (19 June 2017), appendix "Two Feed-Forward Layers = Attention over Parameters"
resources.n: The passage the article cites: the FFN as attention with ReLU for softmax, and Table 5's two attention-over-parameters models (PPL 4.92 and 4.86, BLEU 25.5 and 25.9 against the base model's 4.92 and 25.8). In v2 and v3 only; gone from v4 (30 June 2017) on.

resources.t: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
resources.n: The measurement behind the MLP-as-memory reading: keys in trained FFNs fire on recognisable input patterns, values push the next-token distribution.

resources.t: Understanding Factual Recall in Transformers via Associative Memories
resources.n: The article's footnote 3: when recall only has to pick the right answer from a fixed set (argmax), a d by d matrix holds about d² facts, not d.

resources.t: Hopfield Networks is All You Need
resources.n: Softmax attention as the update rule of a modern Hopfield network with exponential storage capacity: the older form of the article's self-attention section.

resources.t: Test-time regression: a unifying framework for designing sequence models with associative memory
resources.by: Wang, Shi, Fox, 2025 (the author's own paper)
resources.n: The regression objective of the article's optimal-store section, used to derive linear attention, the delta rule and softmax attention as memories written during the forward pass.

resources.t: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers
resources.n: The outer-product store as the state of linear attention, its capacity limit when the sequence outgrows the key dimension, and the delta rule as the fix (footnote 2).

kb.t: Beyond attention: SSMs, Mamba, linear attention, RWKV and hybrids
kb.n: The owner of the outer-product store as a sequence model's state: Fig. 2 writes keys and values into it, Fig. 3 overfills it at small key sizes and fixes it with decay and the delta rule.

kb.t: The transformer from zero: one block, every shape, a GPT you train
kb.n: The block the article rebuilds: attention, the FFN and SwiGLU, and why scores are divided by √d (measured on random vectors).

kb.t: Attention variants: MHA, MQA, GQA, MLA, sliding window, sparse attention and sinks
kb.n: What real models change about the softmax store: shared keys and values, compressed caches, windows and sinks.

kb.t: Linear algebra for ML: vectors to SVD, rank, conditioning, low-rank methods
kb.n: Outer products, least squares and the pseudo-inverse behind the optimal linear store.
YaRN's attention temperature, one of the long-context sharpness rules the article tests.
The paper page; it reads v7, which no longer has the attention-over-parameters appendix.
ReLU, squared ReLU and Swish as activations; this article gives squared ReLU a reason.
